newsitem.title: USA: Minn. Fed takes on critics of U.S. monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Minn. Fed takes on critics of U.S. monetary policy.

text.p: The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis took on critics of the Fed, saying the central bank's monetary policy was aimed at fighting inflation, not curbing economic growth.
"Inflation is bad for economic growth," Minneapolis Fed director of research Arthur Rolnick wrote in an article published in the latest issue of the bank's FedGazette.
"And the Federal Reserve's policy, even though it's often misinterpreted, is an anti-inflation policy, which is another name for a pro-growth policy," Rolnick said.
In a monetarist approach to policy, Rolnick said one of the most robust relationships in all of economics is the long-term relationship between the growth of money and the rate of inflation.
He added, "Right now, money supply is growing a bit fast, it's above our ranges and that raises red flags ...
"If the Fed would put more money in the economy, even if there are currently no signs of price pressures, it would eventually cause inflation."

Rolnick defended the Fed's preemptive monetary policy saying, "The central bank does not have a vendetta against growth, quite the opposite: One of the Fed's goals is to provide the propoer monetary environment for sustained economic growth."
The Fed received sharp criticism for its decision to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, mainly from prominent Republicans on Capitol Hill.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich said in early April that it is "unconscionable" to have the Fed "close off economic growth because of some theoretical model."
The Speaker's scolding of the central bank, analysts said, highlighted his own predicament of wanting to cut taxes while reducing the federal deficit.
Stronger economic growth would help efforts to reduce the budget deficit and provide lawmakers more room to cut taxes, pundits said.
The Fed, however, has cherished its independence over the years and analysts said political pressure has done little or nothing to influence the central bank's decisions on monetary policy.
"The U.S. economy did not create 27 million new jobs over the last 15 years by accident," Rolnick wrote in his article.
"The growth of the 1980's and this decade has been characterized by low inflation, and, if this growth is to continue, the Fed will have to remain vigilant about inflation," he added.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-setting body, is currently deliberating on interest rates. The outcome of the meeting is expected to be announced at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT.
